nameStory: The Spine-shouldered Cellophane Bee gets its name from the tiny spines or projections on its shoulders (thorax), which help distinguish it from its many cellophane bee cousins. All cellophane bees earn their common name from their amazing ability to line their underground nest cells with a clear, waterproof secretion that looks just like cellophane wrap!
description: The Spine-shouldered Cellophane Bee is a small, fuzzy native bee that's part of the plasterer bee family. Like other cellophane bees, it has a compact, robust build with a dark body covered in dense hairs that can appear brownish or grayish depending on the light. These solitary bees are about the size of a small honeybee and are excellent pollinators of native New England plants. Unlike honeybees, each female works alone to create her own underground nest.

idTips.label: Shoulder spines
idTips.description: Look for tiny spines or projections on the shoulders (the area where the wings attach) - these feel slightly rough if you gently touch a specimen and are the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Dense fuzzy coat
idTips.description: The entire body is covered in thick, velvety hairs that feel soft to the touch and can trap pollen, giving the bee a slightly dusty appearance when foraging

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Body appears mostly dark brown to blackish, though the dense hairs can give it a grayish or brownish cast in sunlight

idTips.label: Compact build
idTips.description: Stocky, robust body shape that's noticeably more compact than a honeybee, with a relatively large head compared to body size

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a slightly buzzy, hovering pattern when investigating nest sites, often circling the same area repeatedly

habitat: Look for Spine-shouldered Cellophane Bees in areas with well-drained, sandy or loamy soil where they can easily excavate their underground nests. They favor sunny, open areas like meadows, field edges, gardens, and disturbed soils along trails or roadsides. You'll often spot them near their preferred flowering plants in areas that get good morning sun.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and begin foraging on early spring flowers, with females starting to excavate nest burrows in suitable soil. This is the best time to observe their distinctive hovering behavior over potential nest sites.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you'll see them most frequently visiting flowers and working on their nests. Females are busy provisioning nest cells with pollen and nectar for their developing larvae.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down as the current generation completes development. New adults may emerge late in the season but will overwinter underground until the following spring.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter underground in their natal nests or other protected locations. No surface activity visible during cold months.

funFact: Female cellophane bees produce their nest-lining 'cellophane' by mixing a special glandular secretion that creates a completely waterproof, bacteria-resistant coating - so effective that scientists have studied it for potential applications in food packaging and medical devices!
confusionNotes: With 12 different cellophane bee species in New England, identification can be tricky! The shoulder spines are your best bet for confirming this species. Memory trick: 'Spiny Shoulders Simulans' - feel for those tiny rough projections where other cellophane bees have smooth shoulders.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'simulans' means 'imitating' or 'resembling,' reflecting how similar this species looks to other cellophane bees - which is exactly why those diagnostic shoulder spines are so important for identification! Don't confuse these native cellophane bees with the introduced European honeybee, which has a more golden color and different nesting behavior.
compareHints: Among New England's cellophane bees, the Spine-shouldered stands out primarily due to its namesake shoulder spines, which most relatives lack. It's similar in size and general appearance to the Unequal Cellophane Bee and American Cellophane Bee, but those species have smooth shoulders when examined closely. The specialized shoulder spines make this species one of the easier cellophane bees to identify with confidence.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cellophane bees, the Unequal Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its preference for early spring tree blossoms, especially maples and willows, while relatives like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee specialize in late-season flowers.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the rufous-backed stands out for its prominent rusty-red thoracic hair, while most relatives like the unequal cellophane bee have more subdued brown or gray coloring.

Unlike the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee which specializes on late-summer flowers, or the Aster Cellophane Bee found on fall composites, the Blueberry Cellophane Bee is strictly a spring specialist of heath family plants.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the Aster Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its late-season activity and aster specialization, while the Unequal Cellophane Bee flies much earlier in spring when fruit trees bloom.

Among New England's dozen cellophane bee species, the Broad-footed stands out with its notably wide tarsi, while species like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee or Aster Cellophane Bee are named for their flower preferences rather than physical features.
